transcript:
Header:
Date: 2027-06-05
Time: 11:00 AM PT
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Maya (Redwood SE), Tom (Redwood CSM), Eleanor (Argosy SRE), Marcus (Argosy Head of Platform), Priya (Argosy CTO)

Summary:
Quick follow-up to last week's incident where Argosy saw a sustained latency spike and 5xx errors during a traffic surge after a model rollout. Today's goal: review root cause analysis, agree on mitigations, and assign follow-up tasks (runbook, canary plan, synthetic tests). Transcription is auto-generated and may contain mis-recognitions.

Topics:
- Incident root cause: autoscaler misconfiguration + kernel mismatch after quantized model push
- Immediate mitigations and rollback plan executed
- Long-term reliability improvements: canary rollouts, auto-fallback to lower-capacity model variant, improved tracing and alerting, synthetic traffic harness
- Pricing / Dedicated capacity tradeoffs and SLA adjustments

Transcript:
[00:00:03] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call, we got everybody?
[00:00:10] Eleanor: Yep, here.
[00:00:12] Marcus: Marcus on my side.
[00:00:14] Priya: Priya here.
[00:00:18] Maya: Maya from Redwood, thanks.
[00:00:22] Jordan: So we put together a short RCA doc, Maya, you want to kick us off on the timeline?
[00:00:30] Maya: Yeah, sure. So on 2027-05-29 at ~13:40 UTC, Argosy rolled a quantized variant of the model to reduce token cost and memory pressure. At the same time an autoscaler policy change was deployed that lowered the minimum batch size threshold. The combination led to frequent micro-evictions of GPU workers under bursty traffic which in turn caused high KV cache thrash and warm-up spikes. Essentially more CPU/GPU context switching and cold KV cache fills, and we saw p99 latency jump and an uptick in 5xx errors.
[00:01:05] Eleanor: And to be clear, the errors were mostly timeouts from the front-end LB to the inference service, not application level errors.
[00:01:12] Maya: Right, the logs show request queueing and then abrupt worker recycling. There's also a small mismatch in the kernel selection for that quantized build - some ops fell back to slower kernels on a subset of nodes, likely due to a stale compiled kernel cache after the model artifact changed. Transcription note: it may say "kernel cash" earlier in the doc.
[00:01:37] Marcus: So two correlated issues: autoscaler sensitivity and compiled kernel mismatch. Which one was the primary driver?
[00:01:44] Maya: The autoscaler misconfig was the immediate trigger - it made the cluster oscillate. The kernel mismatch amplified impact on nodes that were still active because they spent extra time on certain ops, increasing latency while the KV cache warmed.
[00:01:58] Priya: Do we have an exact timeline for when the autoscaler policy change was pushed relative to the model push?
[00:02:04] Jordan: Our change logs show they landed within a ~3 minute window; they were independent PRs but got merged back-to-back during the deploy window.
[00:02:12] Tom: We also want to call out that the canary thresholds were conservative but there wasn't an automatic rollback because the health checks were tied to per-node metrics rather than end-to-end p99 latency.
[00:02:24] Eleanor: Right, so we had limited visibility into end-to-end latency in the canary phase which meant the rollout didn't stop early.
[00:02:30] Maya: Correct; so mitigations we executed: immediate revert of the autoscaler policy, manual drain of affected nodes, and a temporary CPU/GPU autoscaling floor increase. We pushed a quick kernel cache invalidation script and warmed the kernels on remaining nodes. That brought errors down in about 18 minutes.
[00:02:51] Priya: Appreciate the quick rollback. On our side we saw customer impact - some downstream billing and support tickets spiked. We need to make sure this doesn't happen in production again.
[00:03:00] Jordan: Absolutely. So longer-term reliability changes proposed: 1) require staggered deploy windows and enforce a 10-minute separation for infra vs model artifact deploys; 2) decouple canary health checks to include end-to-end p99 latency; 3) implement auto-fallback - when p99 crosses threshold fall back to the previous model variant or smaller non-quantized variant; 4) synthetic workload runner to exercise warm paths and KV cache before deploys; 5) improved tracing for kernel selection and compiled-kernel cache state.
[00:03:33] Marcus: For auto-fallback, what's the latency delta between the quantized and fallback variant? Is cost impact acceptable?
[00:03:40] Maya: For normal traffic the quantized model is ~20% cheaper per token, latency is marginally higher p50 but p99 was the issue in cold/warm transitions. Fallback will increase cost slightly but we can flag it as a gated feature for tight-latency paths. We'll include cost estimates in the follow-up.
[00:03:58] Eleanor: We'd like to add synthetic warm-up to our CI so that any model changes are exercised at least at low QPS before rolling to prod.
[00:04:06] Tom: We'll share the synthetic harness repo link and a runbook for Argosy to run. Also plan to add canary checks that query the entire request path.
[00:04:16] Priya: On the SLA side, we want clearer language around fallback and compensation if incidents exceed X minutes of degraded p99. Jordan, can you share suggested contract language?
[00:04:26] Jordan: Yes, I'll draft suggested SLA wording and impact tiers. We'll separate latency SLOs by route and provide clear escalation windows.
[00:04:34] Marcus: What about dedicated capacity? If we move to Redwood Dedicated reserved instances, will that reduce the risk?
[00:04:40] Maya: Dedicated reduces noisy neighbor risk and gives you control over autoscaler behaviors. But dedicated still needs the same canary discipline - the kernel cache mismatch could still happen after model swaps. The advantage is that you can isolate infra-level changes and have deterministic capacity so the oscillation behaviors are more controllable.
[00:04:56] Eleanor: We're interested in a pilot of Dedicated for our most latency-sensitive endpoints. We'll need pricing and a plan for a limited pilot.
[00:05:02] Jordan: I'll add that to next steps; I'll include pricing delta and recommended reserved commit.
[00:05:08] Maya: Quick technical clarifications - the compiled kernel cache invalidation we ran was basically a per-node rm of compiled artifacts and a warm run of the model to recompile kernels. The long-term fix is to ensure the runtime invalidates cache automatically when model checksum changes and to surface kernel-fallback telemetry to alerts.
[00:05:28] Eleanor: Also worth noting: some of our older nodes were still on driver X.Y which had slower code paths. We recommended a coordinated driver/hardware compatibility check pre-deploy.
[00:05:38] Priya: So actionables on infra side: scheduled driver upgrades, staged canaries with end-to-end metrics, synthetic warmers, and an autoscaler safety gate.
[00:05:47] Maya: We'll put a proposed autoscaler safety gate in the config: require stable p99 for 10 minutes during scale-down windows, and a minimum node count floor for bursty traffic. We'll share the exact HCL/JSON diff.
[00:05:58] Marcus: What's the recommended way to detect kernel fallback events in production? Logs? Metrics?
[00:06:03] Maya: We'll emit a metric 'kernel_fallback_rate' and a trace span for kernel selection per request. That way you can create an alert on any non-zero fallback rate during rollouts.
[00:06:12] Tom: I'll add that to the runbook and link to the dashboard.
[00:06:17] Eleanor: Ok, things we need from Redwood: autoscaler diff, synthetic harness, canary health check templates, and updated SLA wording.
[00:06:25] Jordan: And from Argosy: run synthetic tests, agree on pilot scope for Dedicated, and plan driver upgrades.
[00:06:31] Priya: Anything else on risk mitigations?
[00:06:33] Maya: One more - add a pre-deploy checklist gating model artifact changes: verify compiled-kernel signature, run warm-up on a staging pool with identical drivers, then proceed to canary.
[00:06:45] Marcus: We'll also put together a communication plan for customers so support teams can give clear guidance during incidents.
[00:06:51] Jordan: Great. Let's review action items and owners quickly.
[00:06:56] Tom: (reviews action items verbally) Maya will produce config diffs and RCA doc; Jordan to send SLA language and pilot pricing; Tom to update runbook and dashboards; Eleanor to run synthetic tests; Marcus to schedule driver upgrade window.
[00:07:15] Priya: Sounds good, thank you.
[00:07:18] Jordan: OK we'll reconvene after the initial follow-ups - target next sync on 2027-06-14. Thanks all.

End of transcript.
